lessons.title: Professional standards and communication
content: Arrive on time, prepared and fit for duty. Allow enough time to be ready before the vehicle is due to leave.
Follow Swans Travel's dress and presentation standard. Your conduct and appearance represent the company to passengers, clients and the public.
Be polite, calm, helpful and respectful. Do not argue with passengers, colleagues or other road users. If a situation becomes difficult, keep people safe and contact the office.
Never use a handheld phone while driving. Follow company rules for other devices and distractions.
Protect passenger information. Do not share personal details or photographs without permission, including on social media or personal messaging groups.
Safety and legal compliance always come before keeping to a timetable.

slides.heading: You represent Swans Travel
slides.body: A passenger's experience is shaped by the driver they meet. Professional standards are not just about being polite. They include being ready for duty, presenting yourself appropriately, following instructions and making sound decisions throughout the job.
slides.example: Before a school or private hire journey, arrive prepared, check the job information and make sure you understand the collection, destination and any passenger requirements.
slides.takeaway: Be prepared, professional and respectful from the start of every duty.

slides.heading: Communication is part of the job
slides.body: Good communication starts before departure. Confirm the job details, timings, route and any special instructions. During the journey, provide clear and courteous updates and tell the office promptly about delays, route problems or changes. At the end, report completion and anything that needs follow-up.
slides.example: If traffic means you may miss the planned arrival time, tell the office when it is safe to do so. Do not wait until the job has finished.
slides.takeaway: If a detail matters, check it. Do not guess.

slides.heading: Protect passengers and the company's reputation
slides.body: Stay calm if a passenger or road user becomes difficult. Do not argue or allow a disagreement to distract you from driving. Never use a handheld phone while driving. Passenger details and photographs must be kept private and must not be shared without permission.
slides.example: A passenger complains angrily about a delay. Listen, explain what you know accurately and contact the office if the issue needs managing. Do not make promises you cannot authorise.
slides.takeaway: Calm conduct, safe decisions and respect for privacy are expected every time.

lessons.title: End-of-job responsibilities
content: Before leaving the vehicle, park in an authorised safe location and secure it as instructed.
Check the entire passenger saloon for passengers, belongings, damage, cleanliness and anything that may need attention.
Handle lost property through the Swans Travel process. Protect personal information and do not keep items or make informal arrangements with passengers.
Complete job, mileage, defect and incident records accurately and promptly. Include customer concerns and any follow-up required.
Return keys, documents and equipment to the correct place and tell the office when the job is complete.

slides.heading: Finishing a job properly
slides.body: The job is not finished simply because the coach has reached its destination. Park in an authorised safe location and secure the vehicle as instructed. Then check the passenger saloon carefully before leaving it.
slides.example: Walk through the saloon and check seats, floor areas and luggage spaces. Make sure no passenger or belongings have been left behind.
slides.takeaway: Secure the vehicle and check the whole saloon before leaving.

slides.heading: Records, lost property and handover
slides.body: Report lost property through the Swans Travel process and protect personal information. Complete job, mileage, defect and incident records accurately and promptly. Tell the office when the job is complete and flag any customer concern or follow-up action.
slides.example: You find a phone after a journey. Do not keep it or arrange an informal handover. Follow the company lost-property process and report it.
slides.takeaway: Accurate records and a clear handover help the next person do their job.

quiz.question: Before starting a duty, what should a driver confirm?
options: Only the destination
The job details, timings, route and passenger requirements
Only the vehicle registration
Nothing if the route is familiar
quiz.explanation: Confirm the full job information and any special instructions before departure.

quiz.question: A passenger becomes argumentative. What is the professional response?
options: Argue back
Ignore any safety concern
Stay calm, avoid arguing, keep people safe and contact the office if needed
Ask another passenger to deal with it
quiz.explanation: Remain calm and professional. If the situation becomes difficult, prioritise safety and contact the office.

quiz.question: When should a driver report a significant delay or route problem?
options: At the end of the shift only
Promptly during the journey when safe to do so
Only if a passenger complains
Only after reaching the depot
quiz.explanation: The office needs timely information to manage the service and communicate changes.

quiz.question: Which statement about handheld phones is correct?
options: Use it briefly at traffic lights
Use it if the road is quiet
Do not use a handheld phone while driving
Use it for navigation while moving
quiz.explanation: The training material states that drivers must not use a handheld phone while driving.

quiz.question: How should passenger information and photographs be handled?
options: Share useful photos in personal group chats
Post passenger details online if names are hidden
Keep them private and do not share without permission
Send them to friends for advice
quiz.explanation: Passenger information and photographs must be protected.

quiz.question: What should be checked before the journey if a passenger has specific requirements?
options: Assume the previous driver handled it
Wait until the passenger complains
Confirm the requirements and any special instructions
Ask other passengers to decide
quiz.explanation: Check passenger needs and special instructions before departure.

quiz.question: What should happen at the end of a job?
options: Leave without telling anyone
Report completion, incidents, lost property, defects and customer concerns
Only report if the vehicle is damaged
Keep lost property until next shift
quiz.explanation: The office should receive completion information and any follow-up issues.

quiz.question: Where should a coach be parked at the end of a job?
options: Anywhere convenient
In a passenger loading area
In an authorised, safe location, secured as instructed
On the roadside with keys inside
quiz.explanation: Park safely in an authorised place and secure the vehicle.

lessons.title: Vehicle walkaround checks
content: Complete a meaningful walkaround before using the vehicle on the public highway, following the current Swans Travel procedure.
Check tyres and wheels for condition and visible damage. Check lights, mirrors, windows, wipers, bodywork and number plates.
Check doors, emergency exits, steps, handrails, seat belts and passenger areas. Make sure safety equipment is present and accessible.
Look for fluid leaks, visible damage and warning indicators. Check the vehicle's height information and understand its dimensions.
Record the check accurately, including nil defects where the company system requires it. A rushed or tick-box check is not sufficient.
If you are unsure whether an item is safe, ask a competent supervisor before taking the vehicle out.

slides.heading: A walkaround is a safety check, not a tick-box
slides.body: Before using a vehicle on the public highway, complete a meaningful walkaround in line with Swans Travel procedure. Take the time to look at the condition of the vehicle and identify anything that could affect safety or serviceability.
slides.example: A quick glance at the tyres from the cab is not the same as checking the tyres and wheels as part of the walkaround.
slides.takeaway: Look properly, do not assume the vehicle is ready because it was used yesterday.

slides.heading: What to inspect
slides.body: Check tyres and wheels, lights, mirrors, windows, wipers, bodywork and number plates. Check doors, emergency exits, steps, handrails, seat belts and passenger areas. Look for leaks, visible damage and warning indicators, and check required safety equipment.
slides.example: A faulty passenger door, damaged tyre, obstructed exit or visible fluid leak needs attention. Do not dismiss something because the coach appears to drive normally.
slides.takeaway: Check the exterior, passenger areas and safety equipment, not just the obvious items.

slides.heading: Record what you find
slides.body: Record the check accurately, including nil defects where the company system requires it. If you are unsure whether an item is safe, ask a competent supervisor before taking the vehicle out.
slides.example: If you find a defect, record it through the correct system with enough detail for someone else to understand what you found.
slides.takeaway: A good check includes an accurate record and the right follow-up.

lessons.title: Defects and vehicle fitness
content: Never ignore a warning light, unusual noise, vibration, damaged tyre, faulty door or any other condition that may affect safety.
Report defects promptly using the Swans Travel defect process. Give the vehicle ID, time, exact symptoms and location.
Do not take an unroadworthy vehicle onto the road. Do not assume a defect has been cleared because it has been reported.
Wait for the required authorisation before using a vehicle with a reported defect. If you are unsure, ask the responsible person.
If a safety-critical defect develops while in service, stop in a safe place and contact the office. Keep passengers safe while the issue is managed.

slides.heading: Recognise a defect and take it seriously
slides.body: Warning lights, unusual noises, vibration, tyre damage and faulty doors may indicate a safety issue. Do not ignore a symptom because the vehicle still seems to operate. A defect can affect passengers, other road users and the vehicle's fitness for service.
slides.example: A new warning light appears before departure. Do not decide on your own that it is harmless. Report it and follow the defect process.
slides.takeaway: If something changes or does not look or sound right, report it.

slides.heading: Report clearly and wait for clearance
slides.body: Use the Swans Travel defect process. Give the vehicle ID, time, exact symptoms and location. Do not take an unroadworthy vehicle onto the road and do not assume a defect has been cleared just because it has been reported. Wait for the required authorisation.
slides.example: Instead of reporting 'there is a noise', describe when it happens, where it seems to come from and what the vehicle was doing.
slides.takeaway: Report the facts and wait for the correct authorisation.

slides.heading: If a defect develops during a journey
slides.body: If a safety-critical defect develops while in service, stop in a safe place and contact the office. Keep passengers safe while the issue is managed. Do not put yourself or passengers at further risk by attempting an unauthorised inspection or repair.
slides.example: A serious warning appears while carrying passengers. Find a safe place to stop, secure the vehicle and contact the office for instructions.
slides.takeaway: Stop safely, protect passengers and contact the office.

lessons.title: Journey planning and safe driving
content: Read the job sheet or itinerary and confirm collection points, timings, destination, passenger requirements and any special instructions.
Check that the route is suitable for the coach's height, width, length, weight and access requirements. Verify restrictions rather than relying on a sat-nav.
Allow realistic time for traffic, passenger boarding, comfort stops, parking, weather and roadworks. Know the agreed stopping and waiting arrangements.
Use approved sources to check disruption and consider safe alternatives. If the route or plan becomes unsafe or unworkable, stop and contact the office.
Drive defensively: maintain space, match speed to conditions and scan well ahead. Check mirrors regularly and anticipate hazards early.
Remember coach-specific hazards including rear swing, turning circle, longer stopping distances, passenger movement and vulnerable road users.
Avoid reversing where possible. If a trained banksman is used, agree signals first and stop immediately if visual contact or communication is lost. Do not rely only on cameras or sensors.

slides.heading: Prepare before you move
slides.body: Read the job sheet or itinerary. Confirm collection points, timings, destination, passenger requirements and special instructions. Allow realistic time for traffic, boarding, comfort stops and parking.
slides.example: Before leaving the depot, make sure you know where the passengers are being collected and where the coach is expected to wait or park.
slides.takeaway: Know the job and plan the journey before setting off.

slides.heading: The route must suit the coach
slides.body: Check route suitability for the vehicle's height, width, length, weight and access requirements. Consider roadworks, weather, traffic and disruption. A sat-nav is an aid, not the decision-maker. Never follow it into a restriction.
slides.example: A sat-nav offers a shortcut under a bridge but you are unsure of the height limit. Do not attempt it. Verify a suitable route and contact the office if the plan is unclear.
slides.takeaway: The driver remains responsible for checking that the route is suitable.

slides.heading: Drive defensively and manoeuvre safely
slides.body: Maintain space, match speed to conditions and scan well ahead. Remember the coach's rear swing, turning circle and longer stopping distances. Take extra care around cyclists, pedestrians and other vulnerable road users. Avoid reversing where possible. If using a trained banksman, agree signals and stop immediately if contact is lost.
slides.example: If you lose sight of the banksman, stop. Do not continue slowly or rely only on a camera.
slides.takeaway: Plan ahead, leave room to react and stop if a manoeuvre is no longer controlled.

quiz.question: Which items are part of the daily walkaround?
options: Only tyres and fuel
Tyres, wheels, lights, mirrors, windows, wipers and bodywork
Only the passenger seats
Only dashboard warning lights
quiz.explanation: The walkaround includes the vehicle exterior and key safety components.

quiz.question: What should you do if you find a safety-critical defect before departure?
options: Drive slowly to the depot
Ignore it if the vehicle feels normal
Do not use the vehicle, report and record it, then wait for clearance
Ask a passenger whether it looks serious
quiz.explanation: A vehicle with a safety-critical defect must not be used until properly cleared.

quiz.question: What details should be included when reporting a defect?
options: Only the driver's name
Vehicle ID, time, exact symptoms and location
Only a photograph
Only the mileage
quiz.explanation: These details help identify and investigate the defect.

quiz.question: What is the correct approach to a sat-nav route with a height restriction?
options: Follow it because it is designed for vehicles
Try it slowly
Do not follow it into a restriction, verify a suitable route
Ask passengers to watch the roof
quiz.explanation: Sat-nav is an aid, not the decision-maker. Never follow it into a restriction.

quiz.question: What should a driver do if they lose sight of a banksman while reversing?
options: Continue slowly
Use the camera and continue
Stop immediately
Sound the horn and continue
quiz.explanation: Stop if visual contact or communication is lost. Do not guess.

quiz.question: Which approach best describes defensive driving?
options: Drive close to save space
Maintain space, match speed to conditions and scan ahead
Focus only on the vehicle immediately ahead
Keep to the timetable regardless of conditions
quiz.explanation: Space, speed and scan are the defensive driving principles in the training.

quiz.question: What should be checked in the passenger area?
options: Only seat covers
Seats, belts, aisle, steps, handrails, luggage and unobstructed exits
Only heating controls
Only windows
quiz.explanation: The passenger area must be clean, safe and free of obstructions.

quiz.question: What should happen if a safety-critical defect develops while carrying passengers?
options: Continue to the destination
Stop in a safe place and contact the office
Ask passengers to inspect it
Wait until the next scheduled break
quiz.explanation: Stop safely and contact the office, following the defect procedure.

lessons.title: Safe boarding and alighting
content: Stop in a safe, authorised location and secure the vehicle before opening the doors.
Where appropriate, explain the boarding process and offer reasonable assistance. Keep the steps, doors and pavement area clear.
Watch for uneven or wet surfaces and give passengers time to board safely. Do not rush people to recover lost time.
Allow passengers time to sit down and stow belongings before moving. Check that luggage is secure and does not block aisles or exits.
Do not move until doors are closed and it is safe and lawful to depart. Never carry more passengers than the vehicle is authorised and configured to carry.

slides.heading: Create a safe place to board
slides.body: Stop in a safe, authorised location and secure the vehicle before opening the doors. Keep the steps, doors and pavement area clear. Be aware of uneven or wet surfaces and offer reasonable assistance where appropriate.
slides.example: Do not open the doors while the coach is still moving or stopped where passengers would step directly into moving traffic.
slides.takeaway: Safe boarding starts with a safe stopping place and a secured vehicle.

slides.heading: Do not rush passengers
slides.body: Allow passengers time to board, sit down and stow belongings safely. Check luggage is secure and does not block aisles or exits. Do not move until doors are closed and it is safe and lawful to depart.
slides.example: A passenger is still moving down the aisle as the departure time approaches. Wait until it is safe for them to be seated before moving.
slides.takeaway: A timetable never justifies moving before passengers are safe.

lessons.title: Accessibility and additional needs
content: Treat every passenger with dignity, patience and respect, whatever their needs or circumstances.
Ask the passenger what assistance is helpful rather than making assumptions based on appearance.
Follow the vehicle and company procedure for ramps, lifts, wheelchair spaces and securement. Use equipment only in line with your training.
Never improvise a lifting or restraint method. If equipment or training is insufficient, pause and seek help from the office or a trained colleague.
Give clear information and allow extra time where needed. Follow company policy and applicable requirements for assistance animals and mobility equipment.

slides.heading: Ask, do not assume
slides.body: Treat every passenger with dignity, patience and respect. Ask what assistance is helpful rather than making assumptions about what someone can or cannot do. Give clear information and allow extra time where needed.
slides.example: A passenger with a mobility need boards. Ask what assistance they would find useful rather than immediately trying to help in a way they may not want.
slides.takeaway: Respect the passenger and ask what support is appropriate.

slides.heading: Use the right equipment and procedure
slides.body: Follow the vehicle and company procedure for ramps, lifts, wheelchair spaces and securement. Use equipment in line with your training. Never improvise a lifting or restraint method. If equipment or training is insufficient, pause and seek help.
slides.example: You are unsure how to secure mobility equipment. Do not guess or copy an unfamiliar method. Stop and ask a trained colleague or manager.
slides.takeaway: If you are unsure, pause and get help. Never improvise.

quiz.question: When should the vehicle doors be opened for boarding?
options: While still moving slowly
After stopping in a safe authorised place and securing the vehicle
As passengers approach
Before the vehicle has stopped
quiz.explanation: Stop safely and secure the vehicle before opening doors.

quiz.question: Before moving away after boarding, what should the driver ensure?
options: All passengers are standing
Passengers have time to sit, luggage is secure and doors are closed
The timetable is being met
The saloon lights are off
quiz.explanation: Allow passengers to sit and secure luggage before moving.

quiz.question: How should a driver establish what assistance a passenger needs?
options: Assume based on appearance
Ask another passenger
Ask the passenger what assistance would be helpful
Avoid offering any assistance
quiz.explanation: Ask rather than make assumptions, treating passengers with dignity.

quiz.question: What should a driver do if unsure how to use a ramp or securement equipment safely?
options: Try a method they remember seeing
Ask the passenger to work it out
Pause and seek help, do not improvise
Skip the procedure
quiz.explanation: Follow training and company procedures. Never improvise lifting or restraint methods.

quiz.question: A passenger complains about a delay. What is the best response?
options: Argue about the timetable
Promise compensation without authority
Listen, explain accurately and escalate the issue when needed
Ignore the passenger
quiz.explanation: Listen, explain what you know and contact the office about complaints or welfare concerns.

quiz.question: Should passenger safety be compromised to keep to a timetable?
options: Yes, if the delay is significant
Only on private hire
No, safety comes first
Only if passengers agree
quiz.explanation: The training is clear that safety and legal compliance come before the timetable.

quiz.question: How should luggage be placed?
options: In front of emergency exits
Securely, without blocking aisles or exits
On steps if there is no room
Anywhere it fits
quiz.explanation: Luggage must be secure and must not obstruct aisles or exits.

quiz.question: What is the correct way to treat passengers with additional needs?
options: Make decisions without asking
With dignity, patience and respect, asking what help is useful
Avoid speaking to them
Ask other passengers to assist without consent
quiz.explanation: Treat every passenger with dignity and ask what assistance is helpful.

lessons.title: Drivers’ hours and tachographs
content: Know which drivers' hours rules apply to the specific operation. Domestic, assimilated and AETR rules may differ.
Use the tachograph correctly and make accurate mode and activity entries. Make sure records reflect the work actually carried out.
Plan driving, breaks and rest before the journey. Do not rely on memory or guesswork, and check the rules that apply to the duty.
Never manipulate, falsify, conceal or ask anyone else to alter tachograph records improperly.
Tell the office or responsible manager early if delays threaten legal hours or planned rest. Follow instructions and the applicable rules.
This module is a reminder, not a substitute for checking current DVSA guidance and Swans Travel operating procedures.

slides.heading: Know which rules apply to your duty
slides.body: Different operations may be subject to different drivers' hours rules, including domestic, assimilated or AETR rules. Identify which rules apply to the specific operation and follow current guidance and Swans Travel procedures.
slides.example: Do not assume that the rules from yesterday's duty automatically apply to today's job. Check the operation and the applicable requirements.
slides.takeaway: Know the rules that apply before you start the duty.

slides.heading: Use the tachograph accurately
slides.body: Use the tachograph correctly and make accurate mode and activity entries. Records must reflect the work actually carried out. Never manipulate, falsify or conceal records or ask anyone else to alter them improperly.
slides.example: If an activity needs recording, make the correct entry rather than relying on memory or asking someone to change it later.
slides.takeaway: Tachograph records must be accurate and honest.

slides.heading: Plan, monitor and communicate
slides.body: Plan driving, breaks and rest before the journey. Do not rely on memory or guesswork. If traffic or another delay may affect legal hours or planned rest, tell the office or responsible manager early and follow the applicable rules.
slides.example: You can see that congestion may put the planned schedule at risk. Contact the office promptly, while safe to do so, rather than waiting until you reach a limit.
slides.takeaway: Plan ahead and raise a potential hours problem early.

lessons.title: Fitness for duty
content: Start work fit, alert and able to carry out the duty safely. Fatigue can affect judgement, concentration and reaction time.
Tell the appropriate manager if illness, fatigue or medication may affect your ability to drive safely. Do not hide a concern.
Never drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs.
Follow company rules on mobile phones, smoking, eating and other distractions. Keep attention on driving and passenger safety.
Take required breaks and raise fatigue concerns early. Do not allow pressure to keep to a timetable to override fitness for duty.

slides.heading: Be fit and alert for duty
slides.body: Start work fit, alert and able to carry out the duty safely. Fatigue can affect concentration and judgement. Take required breaks and raise fatigue concerns early.
slides.example: You feel unusually tired before a duty. Do not hide it or assume you will be fine once you start. Raise the concern with the appropriate manager.
slides.takeaway: Being fit for duty is a safety responsibility.

slides.heading: Raise anything that may affect safe driving
slides.body: Tell the appropriate manager if illness, fatigue or medication may affect your ability to drive safely. Never drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs. Follow company rules on phones, smoking, eating and other distractions.
slides.example: A new medication makes you feel drowsy. Tell the appropriate manager and do not undertake driving if you may be unsafe.
slides.takeaway: Be honest about fitness and remove avoidable distractions.

quiz.question: What must a driver know about drivers’ hours rules?
options: Only the rules used on the last job
Which rules apply to the specific operation
Only the rules for local journeys
The rules do not change by operation
quiz.explanation: Domestic, assimilated and AETR rules may differ, so identify the rules for the duty.

quiz.question: How should tachograph activity entries be made?
options: Only when asked by a manager
Accurately, using the correct mode and activity
At the end of the week from memory
Use whichever mode is quickest
quiz.explanation: The tachograph must be used correctly with accurate mode and activity entries.

quiz.question: What should a driver do if traffic delays may affect legal hours or planned rest?
options: Wait until the limit is reached
Tell the office early and follow the applicable rules
Continue and explain later
Change the tachograph record
quiz.explanation: Raise the issue early so the operation can be managed safely and legally.

quiz.question: Which action is prohibited?
options: Planning breaks
Making accurate entries
Manipulating, falsifying or concealing tachograph records
Checking which rules apply
quiz.explanation: Records must not be manipulated, falsified or concealed.

quiz.question: What should a driver do if medication may affect safe driving?
options: Say nothing
Take extra care but do not tell anyone
Tell the appropriate manager
Drive until symptoms become severe
quiz.explanation: Drivers should raise illness, fatigue or medication concerns that may affect safety.

quiz.question: Which statement about alcohol and drugs is correct?
options: It is acceptable after a long rest
Only illegal drugs are prohibited
Never drive under their influence
It is acceptable if the route is short
quiz.explanation: The training states never drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

quiz.question: What should be planned before a journey?
options: Only fuel stops
Driving, breaks and rest, using the rules that apply
Only passenger collection times
Nothing if the job is familiar
quiz.explanation: Plan driving, breaks and rest rather than relying on memory or guesswork.

quiz.question: What takes priority if a timetable conflicts with legal compliance?
options: The timetable
Passenger pressure
Legal compliance and safety
The driver's preferred arrival time
quiz.explanation: Safety and legal compliance come before keeping to a timetable.

lessons.title: Breakdown, collision or serious incident
content: Stop in the safest available place, secure the vehicle and assess immediate danger.
Contact emergency services where required. Give the location and nature of the incident clearly and follow emergency-service instructions.
Follow the Swans Travel emergency or breakdown procedure and contact the office as soon as it is safe to do so.
Keep passengers together in a safe place away from moving traffic and other hazards. Consider anyone who may need assistance.
Do not put yourself or passengers at further risk to inspect or repair the vehicle.
When safe, record factual details, witnesses and actions taken. Avoid speculation or assigning blame.

slides.heading: Make the scene as safe as possible
slides.body: After a breakdown, collision or serious incident, stop in the safest available place, secure the vehicle and assess immediate danger. Protect life first and follow emergency-service instructions.
slides.example: If the coach stops in a dangerous position, focus first on immediate safety and the passengers, not on diagnosing the mechanical problem.
slides.takeaway: Stop safely, secure the vehicle and assess danger first.

slides.heading: Call for the right help
slides.body: Contact emergency services where required and clearly give the location and nature of the incident. Follow the Swans Travel emergency or breakdown procedure and contact the office as soon as it is safe.
slides.example: When speaking to emergency services, give a clear location and explain what has happened. Do not delay an emergency call when it is required.
slides.takeaway: Use emergency services when needed and notify the office when safe.

slides.heading: Look after passengers and record facts
slides.body: Keep passengers together in a safe place away from moving traffic and other hazards. Do not put yourself or passengers at further risk to inspect or repair the vehicle. When safe, record factual details, witnesses and actions taken.
slides.example: Do not stand passengers beside a coach in a hazardous location just because it is convenient. Follow the safest available arrangements.
slides.takeaway: Passenger welfare comes first. Record facts when it is safe.

lessons.title: Fire and evacuation
content: Know the location and operation of emergency exits and the vehicle's safety equipment. Follow vehicle-specific training and procedures.
If evacuation is required, give passengers short, clear instructions and direct them to a safe assembly point away from traffic.
Do not re-enter a vehicle or retrieve belongings if there is danger.
Account for passengers where possible and report anyone missing or needing assistance.
Do not attempt firefighting unless you are trained, it is safe, and the correct equipment and an escape route are available.

slides.heading: Know the vehicle's emergency arrangements
slides.body: Know the location and operation of emergency exits and the vehicle's safety equipment. Follow the vehicle-specific evacuation procedure and your training.
slides.example: Before an emergency happens, familiarise yourself with the exits and equipment on the vehicle you are driving.
slides.takeaway: Know the vehicle and follow its evacuation procedure.

slides.heading: Give clear evacuation instructions
slides.body: If evacuation is required, give passengers short, clear instructions and direct them to a safe assembly point away from traffic. Do not re-enter the vehicle or retrieve belongings if there is danger.
slides.example: Use clear instructions that passengers can act on. Direct them away from the vehicle and traffic rather than allowing people to gather around it.
slides.takeaway: Move people to safety and do not send anyone back into danger.

slides.heading: Account for passengers and act within your training
slides.body: Account for passengers where possible and report anyone missing or needing assistance. Do not attempt firefighting unless you are trained, it is safe, and the correct equipment and an escape route are available.
slides.example: Do not attempt to fight a fire simply because an extinguisher is nearby. Your training, the conditions and a safe escape route all matter.
slides.takeaway: Do not take risks beyond your training or the safe conditions.

quiz.question: What is the first priority after a breakdown or serious incident?
options: Call the depot while still moving
Unload passengers immediately into traffic
Stop in the safest available place, secure the vehicle and assess immediate danger
Inspect the engine before checking passengers
quiz.explanation: First make the situation as safe as possible and assess immediate danger.

quiz.question: When should emergency services be contacted?
options: Only after the office gives permission
Where required by the situation
Only if another driver asks
Never, the office handles everything
quiz.explanation: Contact emergency services where required and give clear location and incident details.

quiz.question: Where should passengers be kept after an incident?
options: Beside the coach on the carriageway
Together in a safe place away from moving traffic and hazards
Free to walk around the scene
Inside the vehicle regardless of danger
quiz.explanation: Keep passengers together and away from traffic or other hazards.

quiz.question: What should a driver do before attempting to inspect or repair a damaged vehicle?
options: Attempt a repair immediately
Ask passengers to help
Avoid any action that puts themselves or passengers at further risk
Stand in the live carriageway to inspect it
quiz.explanation: Do not create further risk while inspecting or repairing a vehicle.

quiz.question: What instructions should be given during an evacuation?
options: Long explanations before moving
Short, clear instructions directing passengers to a safe assembly point
Tell passengers to collect their belongings first
Let passengers choose any direction
quiz.explanation: Give clear instructions and move people to a safe assembly point away from traffic.

quiz.question: Should anyone re-enter a vehicle to retrieve belongings when there is danger?
options: Yes, if belongings are valuable
Only if the passenger asks
No
Only after the driver has left
quiz.explanation: Do not re-enter a vehicle or retrieve belongings if there is danger.

quiz.question: When may a driver attempt firefighting?
options: Whenever a fire is small
Only if trained, it is safe and correct equipment and an escape route are available
If passengers ask
Before raising the alarm
quiz.explanation: Firefighting is conditional on training, safety, suitable equipment and an escape route.

quiz.question: What should be recorded after an incident when it is safe to do so?
options: Opinions and blame
Only the vehicle registration
Factual details, witnesses and actions taken
Nothing if emergency services attended
quiz.explanation: Record factual details, witnesses and actions taken when safe.

lessons.title: Practical scenarios
content: Scenario: a new warning light appears while passengers are on board. Stop in a safe place, assess immediate risk and follow the company defect procedure. Contact the office and do not continue if the vehicle may be unsafe.

Scenario: a sat-nav suggests a shortcut but you are unsure about a height restriction. Do not proceed until the restriction and route are verified. The sat-nav does not override vehicle dimensions or approved route planning.
Scenario: you lose sight of a banksman while reversing. Stop immediately. Only continue when safe communication and visual contact are re-established.
Scenario: traffic delays may affect legal hours or planned rest. Contact the office or responsible manager promptly and follow the rules that apply to the duty.
Scenario: a passenger is upset about a delay. Stay calm, listen and explain accurately. Do not promise something you cannot authorise or compromise safety to recover time.
Scenario: you are unsure how to assist a passenger safely. Pause, do not improvise a lift or restraint, and ask a trained colleague or manager for help.

slides.heading: Scenario: a warning light appears
slides.body: A new warning light appears while passengers are on board. Do not ignore it or assume it is harmless. Stop in a safe place, assess immediate risk and follow the company defect procedure. Contact the office and do not continue if the vehicle may be unsafe.
slides.example: Think through the order: safe stopping place, secure the vehicle, passenger welfare, contact the office and follow instructions.
slides.takeaway: Stop safely and follow the defect process.

slides.heading: Scenario: an uncertain low bridge
slides.body: Your sat-nav suggests a shortcut but you are unsure about the height restriction. Do not proceed until the restriction and route are verified. The sat-nav does not override the vehicle's dimensions or approved route planning.
slides.example: What would you do if the road is narrow and there is nowhere safe to turn around? This is why route suitability must be checked before entering a restricted area.
slides.takeaway: Never guess with a height or weight restriction.

slides.heading: Scenario: reversing and fatigue
slides.body: If you lose sight of a banksman, stop immediately. If traffic delays may affect legal hours or planned rest, contact the office or responsible manager promptly and follow the rules that apply to the duty.
slides.example: In both situations, continuing and hoping for the best increases risk. Stop or raise the concern before it becomes worse.
slides.takeaway: Stop when control or communication is lost. Raise hours concerns early.

slides.heading: Scenario: passenger complaint or uncertainty
slides.body: If a passenger is upset about a delay, stay calm, listen and explain accurately. Do not promise something you cannot authorise or compromise safety to recover time. If you are unsure how to assist a passenger safely, pause and seek help rather than improvising.
slides.example: A passenger asks you to use an unsafe stopping place to save them a walk. Explain calmly and follow the safe arrangements.
slides.takeaway: Be helpful, but never compromise safety or act outside your training.

lessons.title: Knowledge check and sign-off
content: Complete the module knowledge check and discuss any incorrect answers with the trainer. Each module assessment requires 100% to demonstrate the required knowledge.
If an answer is incorrect, review the explanation and the relevant lesson, then retake the assessment. Further coaching should be provided where needed.
Record the topics covered, practical checks required, actions outstanding, knowledge outcome, practical assessment outcome and review date.
A driver signature confirms attendance or discussion. It does not replace a competent practical assessment or manager review.
Use the current DVSA guidance, Swans Travel procedures, vehicle handbook and operator instructions. This company induction is not an approved Driver CPC course.

slides.heading: What the assessment is checking
slides.body: The module knowledge check is there to confirm that you understand the training, not to replace it. Work through the lessons, consider the examples and use the interactive decisions to practise applying the information.
slides.example: If a question feels unfamiliar, revisit the lesson and understand why the safe response is correct before trying again.
slides.takeaway: Learn the material first. The quiz confirms your understanding.

slides.heading: How completion works
slides.body: Each module assessment requires 100%. If an answer is incorrect, review the explanation and the relevant lesson, then retake the assessment. Further coaching should be provided where needed.
slides.example: You score 7 out of 8. The module remains in progress. Review the incorrect answer and try again when you understand the subject.
slides.takeaway: A module is passed only when every question is correct.

slides.heading: Training records and practical sign-off
slides.body: Record the topics covered, practical checks required, actions outstanding, knowledge outcome, practical assessment outcome and review date. A driver signature confirms attendance or discussion. It does not replace a competent practical assessment or manager review.
slides.example: Passing the online quiz does not prove a driver can complete a walkaround or safely manoeuvre a coach. Those practical skills still need appropriate assessment.
slides.takeaway: Online learning supports training, it does not replace practical competence checks.

quiz.question: A new warning light appears while carrying passengers. What should the driver do?
options: Continue to the destination
Stop in a safe place, assess the risk and follow the defect procedure
Switch off the display
Ask passengers to decide
quiz.explanation: Treat a new warning as a potential defect, stop safely and follow the company procedure.

quiz.question: A sat-nav suggests a shortcut but the height restriction is uncertain. What is the correct decision?
options: Follow the sat-nav slowly
Ask a passenger to check the bridge
Do not proceed until the route and restriction are verified
Try the route if no other traffic is present
quiz.explanation: Never follow sat-nav into an unverified height or weight restriction.

quiz.question: You lose sight of the banksman while reversing. What do you do?
options: Continue slowly
Stop immediately and re-establish safe communication
Rely on the reversing camera
Sound the horn and continue
quiz.explanation: Stop immediately if visual contact or communication is lost.

quiz.question: Traffic delays may affect your legal hours. What should happen next?
options: Keep driving and report it later
Alter the tachograph entry
Contact the office or responsible manager promptly
Ignore the issue if passengers are waiting
quiz.explanation: Raise the issue early and follow the rules that apply to the duty.

quiz.question: A passenger is angry about a delay. What should you prioritise?
options: Promise an arrival time you cannot guarantee
Argue that the delay is not your fault
Stay calm, explain accurately and never compromise safety
Drive faster to recover time
quiz.explanation: Listen and explain accurately, but never put passenger safety at risk.

quiz.question: You are unsure how to assist a passenger safely. What should you do?
options: Try a lifting method you have seen before
Ask another passenger to lift them
Pause and seek help rather than improvising
Ignore the request
quiz.explanation: Do not improvise lifting or restraint methods. Seek help if unsure.

quiz.question: What does a driver signature on the training record confirm?
options: That the driver is competent in every task
Attendance and discussion, not a substitute for practical assessment
That no further training is needed
That the manager has completed the assessment
quiz.explanation: The source presentation explicitly says a signature does not replace competent practical assessment.

quiz.question: What should happen if a knowledge check is not passed?
options: Mark the module complete anyway
Remove the incorrect questions
Further coaching and another attempt before module completion
Sign off the driver without review
quiz.explanation: A failed assessment means the driver needs to revisit the material and demonstrate the required knowledge.

assessment.completionRule: Every module quiz must score 100% before the module can be marked complete.
